title: Practice set 1
origin: icanspeak Spanish: all texts, tasks and listening scripts written by us (2026-10-30).
sourcing: The structure, number of tasks, task types and timings follow Cambridge English B1 Preliminary (Handbook for teachers, 2020 format). All texts, tasks and listening scripts here are our own; nothing is copied from a Cambridge exam paper. The real exam uses pictures in some tasks; here they are short text descriptions. People, places and businesses are invented. The listening scripts are voiced with speech synthesis. B1 Preliminary is © Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

scoring.note: Cambridge English B1 Preliminary gives one overall score on the Cambridge English Scale: 140-159 is a B1 pass (Grade C 140-152, Grade B 153-159) and 160-170 is Grade A, shown at B2 level. Each skill also gets its own scale score. Writing and Speaking are marked by examiners on set criteria. The 60 % line is our own guide for this practice set, not an official pass mark.

parts.title: Short real-world texts
parts.instruction: Read the five short texts. For each question 1-5, choose the correct answer A, B or C.

texts.label: Text 1
texts.title: Notice in a library
paras: From Monday 3 March the library will close at 6 pm instead of 8 pm on weekdays while the heating is repaired. The children’s section will stay open until 7 pm. Books can still be returned at any time through the box next to the front door.

texts.label: Text 2
texts.title: Text message
paras: Hi Ben, I’m running about 15 minutes late. Start without me and order me a coffee? The same as last time, please. Parking here is a nightmare! Zoe

texts.label: Text 3
texts.title: Sign at a swimming pool
paras: Please shower before you swim. Children under 10 must be with an adult in the pool area. The pool is closed for cleaning every Tuesday morning.

texts.label: Text 4
texts.title: Email from a school
paras: Dear parents, the trip to the science museum on Friday will go ahead, even though the weather forecast is poor. Please make sure your child brings a waterproof coat and a packed lunch. We will leave school at 9 am and be back by 3.30 pm. Mrs Clarke

texts.label: Text 5
texts.title: Sign in a bakery window
paras: Bella’s Bakery: buy any loaf before 10 am and get a free cup of tea or coffee. This offer is not available on Sundays.

items.question: What is the notice about?
options: The library will be closed all week.
The library will close earlier for a while.
items.why: Weekday closing moves from 8 pm to 6 pm 'while the heating is repaired', so it is temporary. Only the children's section stays open later.

items.question: Why is Zoe writing to Ben?
options: To ask him to find a parking space
To tell him she will arrive later than planned
To change the place where they will meet
items.why: She is 15 minutes late. Parking is only a complaint, and the place is not changed.

items.question: What does the sign say about children under 10?
options: They can only swim on Tuesday mornings.
They must wear a swimming cap.
They must be with an adult in the pool area.
items.why: Tuesday morning is when the pool is closed, and caps are not mentioned.

items.question: What are parents asked to do?
options: Pick their children up from the museum
Decide whether their child goes on the trip
Send their child with a waterproof coat and a packed lunch
items.why: The trip is going ahead and the children travel with the school, so parents only need to pack a coat and lunch.

items.question: What can customers get at Bella's Bakery?
options: A free drink if they buy bread early in the day
A free loaf if they buy a hot drink
items.why: The offer is a free tea or coffee with a loaf bought before 10 am. It is not available on Sundays.

parts.title: Matching people to activities
parts.instruction: The five people below (6-10) each want to find an activity. Read the descriptions A-H of eight activities. Decide which activity (A-H) is the most suitable for each person. For questions 6-10, choose the correct letter A-H. There are three activities that you do not need to use.

a.title: A  Italian cooking evenings
a.body: Learn to cook three classic dishes in a friendly group, then sit down and eat them together. Tuesdays and Thursdays, 6.30-8.30 pm. £25 per evening.

b.title: B  River boat trip
b.body: Sit on the covered deck while our guide tells you the history of the town’s mills and bridges. No walking needed. Daily at 11 am and 2 pm. 90 minutes. £12.

c.title: C  Family pottery studio
c.body: Saturdays, 2-4 pm. Children aged six and over make a bowl or a mug together with an adult. We bake it for you and you collect it the following week. £18 per pair.

d.title: D  Early birds running club
d.body: Wednesday mornings at 6.30 am in Mill Park. All speeds welcome and completely free. Finish in time for work.

e.title: E  Sunday sounds
e.body: Free live music by local bands in the market square, 1-4 pm every Sunday. Bring a chair and a picnic.

f.title: F  Castle hill walking tour
f.body: A three-hour guided walk to the castle ruins, starting Sunday at 10 am. Very steep steps and uneven paths. £8.

g.title: G  Weekend photography course
g.body: Two full days, Saturday and Sunday, 9 am-5 pm, for adults. Bring your own camera. £90.

h.title: H  Bike hire
h.body: Hire a bike from £10 a day. Helmets included. Open 9 am-5 pm every day.

items.prompt: Marta works until 6 pm and has weekends free for her family. During the week she would like to learn to cook something new and enjoy eating it afterwards.
Dev loves local history, but he has a bad knee and cannot manage steps or long walks. He would like to do something on a weekday morning or afternoon.
Hannah would like to do something creative with her eight-year-old daughter on a Saturday afternoon.
Tom wants to get fitter by running before he starts work in the morning. He does not want to spend any money.
Amara wants to hear some live music on Sunday afternoon, but she is saving money at the moment.

parts.title: A magazine article
parts.instruction: Read the article about learning to swim. For each question 11-15, choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.

texts.label: Magazine article
texts.title: Swimming at forty-two
paras: When I turned forty-two, I could not swim. For years I had told people that I just didn’t like water, but the truth was that I was afraid of it. When I was seven, I fell into the deep end of a hotel pool and had to be pulled out by a lifeguard. After that I stayed at the side of every pool party and beach holiday, and I always had an excuse ready.

What changed things was my daughter, Lucy. Last spring her school announced a trip to an outdoor activity centre with canoeing, and she came home worried because she had never been in a boat. I wanted to say, “Don’t worry, Mum will come too.” Then I realised that I would not be able to get into a boat myself. I did not want her to grow up as nervous as I was, so I decided to do something about it.

I found a class for adult beginners at the leisure centre on Monday evenings. I almost didn’t go in. I sat in the car park for ten minutes, until another woman knocked on my window and said, “Are you here for the swimming class? I’m terrified too.” That was Priya, and we have been friends ever since.

The first lesson was just standing in the shallow end and putting our faces in the water. It sounds easy, but I found it harder than anything I do at work. Our teacher, Sam, never hurried us. He told us to think of each lesson as one small step and not to worry about the next one. After six weeks I could float on my back, and after four months I swam a whole length without stopping. I cried a little in the water, which was lucky because nobody could tell.

I’m not a good swimmer yet. I’m slow, and I still hold my nose when I jump in. But last month Lucy and I went canoeing together at her school’s activity centre, and I wore a life jacket and enjoyed every minute. If you have been avoiding something because you are afraid, my advice is to find someone who is afraid of it too. It is much easier to be brave in a pair.

items.question: Why did the writer say for years that she did not like water?
options: She had never had the chance to learn.
Something frightening happened to her as a child.
She disliked pool parties and beach holidays.
Her family never went near water.
items.why: She fell into a deep pool aged seven and had to be pulled out. The excuses came after that, not before.

items.question: Why did the writer decide to learn to swim?
options: She did not want her daughter to grow up with the same fear.
Her daughter asked her to join a school trip.
Her doctor told her to take up exercise.
She was invited to a pool party.
items.why: Lucy was worried about the canoe trip, and the writer says she did not want her to grow up as nervous as she was. Lucy did not ask her to come.

items.question: What happened in the car park?
options: The writer decided to go home.
The swimming teacher came to meet her.
items.why: Priya knocked on her window, and the writer went in. They only became friends afterwards.

items.question: What does the writer say about the teacher, Sam?
options: He kept the lessons very short.
He was strict about being on time.
He told the group about his own fears.
He told them to take one small step at a time.
items.why: Sam told them to treat each lesson as one small step and not to worry about the next.

items.question: What is the writer's main purpose in the last paragraph?
options: To describe how good a swimmer she has become
To complain about the cost of lessons
To encourage readers who are afraid of something
To explain how to canoe safely
items.why: She says she is not a good swimmer yet, and the paragraph ends with advice for anyone avoiding something they fear.

parts.title: Sentences removed from an article
parts.instruction: Five sentences have been removed from the article about volunteering. Choose from the sentences A-H the one which fits each gap (16-20). There are three extra sentences which you do not need to use.
parts.textTitle: Two weeks at an animal rescue centre

bank.a: To my surprise, the little girl chose Biscuit.
bank.b: In the end, I agreed to stay for a third week.
bank.c: A friend of mine had done the same thing the year before and told me it was the best holiday she had ever had.
bank.d: He had been badly treated by his first owner and was afraid of strangers.
bank.e: The cats, on the other hand, spent most of the day asleep in the sun.
bank.f: There were about thirty dogs, twenty cats and a few rabbits living there.
bank.g: Gwen says the centre needs new volunteers every summer.
bank.h: My arms ached and my feet hurt, and I fell asleep as soon as I got into bed each night.

segments.t: Last summer I spent two weeks volunteering at an animal rescue centre near Bristol.
I had never worked with animals before, so I was nervous when I arrived on the first morning.
The manager, a tall woman called Gwen, showed me round.
My job was to feed the dogs twice a day and to clean their kennels.
At first the work was harder than I expected. I started at seven every morning and often did not finish until after six.
By the end of the first week, though, I hardly noticed the tiredness.
The dog I got to know best was an old brown terrier called Biscuit.
I spent my free half-hours sitting quietly next to his kennel, and after a few days he let me stroke him.
On my last day, a family came to the centre looking for a pet.
I was sad to say goodbye, but I was also very happy for him. I am going back next summer.

items.why: It explains why she went and leads into 'I had never worked with animals before'.
It tells us what the centre looks like, before her job with the dogs is described.
It describes the tiredness that 'I hardly noticed' refers to in the next sentence.
'He' is Biscuit, and the sentence explains why she has to sit quietly next to him.
The family are looking for a pet, and the next sentence shows she says goodbye to the dog they chose.

parts.title: Vocabulary in an email
parts.instruction: Read the email from Jo to a friend. Choose the correct word for each space (21-26). For each question, choose the correct answer A, B, C or D.

segments.t: Dear Maya,
Thank you for your email! I am writing from my new flat in Leeds. It is small, but it has a lovely
of the park. I share it with a girl called Ana, who works at the hospital. We have already
friends, even though we only see each other at weekends.
My new job at the bookshop is going well. The journey from the flat to the shop
about twenty minutes by bus, so I can read on the way. At the weekend I am going to
around the old town, because I have not seen much of it yet. Everything is more expensive than at home, so I am trying not to
too much money on takeaway food.
Please
me know when you can visit. There is a sofa bed in the living room, and you can stay as long as you like.
Best wishes,
Jo

items.why: We say 'a view of' a park or a garden.
The fixed phrase is 'make friends'.
A journey 'takes' a certain amount of time.
'Look around' a place means to walk around it and see it.
'Spend money on' something. 'Pay' would need 'for'.
The fixed phrase is 'let me know'.

parts.title: Open cloze: a day at the seaside
parts.instruction: Read the text about a day out. Write ONE word for each gap (27-32). Use only one word in each gap.

segments.t: Last Saturday I went to the seaside
my cousin, Dan. We had planned to go swimming, but the water was
cold that we decided to walk along the beach instead. While we were walking, it began
rain.
Luckily, we found a small café,
we sat for an hour and drank hot chocolate. Dan said it was one
the best days he had had for a long time. He has promised to take me again as soon
the weather gets warmer.

items.why: 'Go somewhere with someone' means together.
'so cold that' shows the result: they decided to walk instead.
'It began to rain.'
'where' refers back to the café as a place.
'one of the best days'.
'as soon as' means 'when' in a promise about the future.

parts.title: Email: answer a friend
parts.instruction: This is Part 1 and you must answer it. Read the email from your friend Sam and the four notes. Write an email to Sam using all the notes. Write about 100 words. You have about 20 minutes.

tasks.title: Question 1 · Email to Sam
tasks.situation: Your English friend Sam has sent you this email: “Hi! I’m planning a birthday dinner for my sister next Saturday. Would you like to come? I can’t decide where we should eat. Do you have any ideas? Sam”
tasks.prompt: Write your email to Sam. Use all the notes.
points: Thank Sam and say you would like to come.
Suggest a restaurant and say why it is a good choice.
Say you can only arrive after 7.30 pm and give a reason.
Ask whether you should bring a present for Sam’s sister.
tasks.model:
Hi Sam,
Thanks so much for the invitation. I’d love to come to your sister’s birthday dinner!
How about going to the Olive Tree? It’s a small Italian restaurant near the station, and the pasta there is really good. It isn’t too expensive either, which is important for a big group.
I’m afraid I can’t get there before 7.30, because I finish work at seven and I need to go home and change first. Please start without me if I’m a little late!
Shall I bring a present for your sister, or are you all giving her one together? Let me know.
See you on Saturday,
Marco
checklist: Content: all four notes are answered (thanks and yes, restaurant with a reason, arrival time with a reason, question about a present).
Communicative achievement: friendly, informal tone suited to a friend (Hi Sam, Thanks so much, See you on Saturday).
Organisation: greeting, short paragraphs in a logical order, a closing line; linking words such as because, but, and.
Language: suggestions (How about + -ing), a polite question (Shall I bring …?), B1 vocabulary for food and plans.
Length: about 100 words; much shorter usually means a note is missed.

parts.title: Article or story
parts.instruction: Choose one of the questions below (2A or 2B) and write about 100 words. You have about 25 minutes.

tasks.title: Question 2A · Article
tasks.situation: You see this announcement in an English-language magazine: “Articles wanted: My favourite way to relax. What do you do to relax, and why do you enjoy it? Write us an article. We will publish the best ones next month.”
points: Say what you do to relax.
tasks.model:
My favourite way to relax
After a long week at work, my favourite way to relax is cooking. I know that sounds like more work, but for me it is the opposite.
On Sunday afternoons I put on some music, open the window and make something new. Last week it was a vegetable curry. I enjoy it because I can’t think about my emails while I’m chopping onions!
Cooking also gives me something at the end: a meal for my family or friends. We all sit down together and talk for hours.
If you have never tried it, start with something simple, like soup. You may find that you enjoy it too.
checklist: Content: you say what you do, why you enjoy it, and you give a tip.
Communicative achievement: a title and a lively, friendly tone for magazine readers.
Organisation: introduction, middle, short ending; paragraphs.
Language: present simple for habits, because, but, so; some interesting words, not only 'good' and 'nice'.
Length: about 100 words.

tasks.title: Question 2B · Story
tasks.situation: Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence: “When Tom opened the door, he could not believe what he saw.”
points: Say what Tom saw and what happened next.
tasks.model:
When Tom opened the door, he could not believe what he saw. His kitchen was full of friends, balloons and a huge chocolate cake.
“Surprise!” everybody shouted.
Tom had come home early from work because he felt tired and a little sad. He thought that everyone had forgotten his thirtieth birthday. In fact, his sister had planned the party for weeks, and she had asked his neighbour for the key.
Tom laughed and hugged her. Then he blew out the candles, and everybody sang. It was the best birthday he had ever had, and he promised himself never to feel sad about it again.
checklist: Content: the first sentence is used exactly; what Tom saw and the ending are clear.
Communicative achievement: the story is easy to follow and interesting.
Organisation: beginning, middle and end; time words such as then, in fact, after that.
Language: past simple and past perfect (had planned), direct speech, B1 vocabulary for feelings.
Length: about 100 words.

parts.title: Seven short recordings
parts.instruction: You will hear seven short recordings. For each question 1-7, choose the correct answer A, B or C. You will hear each recording twice. In the real exam the options are pictures; here they are short descriptions.

script.t: Shall we meet at half past six outside the cinema?
I don’t finish work until six, and the bus takes forty minutes, so I’d be late. Could we say seven instead?
Seven is fine. The film doesn’t start until eight, so there’s plenty of time.

Hi Jade, it’s Tom. I went to the shop on Saturday. I was going to buy the blue jacket, but they didn’t have my size, so I got the green one instead. I looked at some boots as well, but they were really expensive, so I’ll wait for the sale. Call me later.
Ticket office, can I help you?
Hello. I think I left my umbrella on the quarter past nine train from Manchester. It’s black, with a wooden handle.
Let me look. Oh yes, the guard handed one in this morning. Normally we send things to the lost property office, but that’s closed until Monday, so I’m keeping it here with me at the ticket office.
Oh, that’s lucky. I’ll come at lunchtime.

And now the weather. Friday will be warm and sunny all day, so make the most of it. On Saturday the morning stays dry, but clouds will move in from the west and bring rain by the afternoon. Sunday looks dry again, but it will be quite windy, especially near the coast.
Is that your old bike in the garage? It looks fine. Have you thought about selling it?
I did, but advertising it online takes ages. Anyway, my nephew has just learnt to ride, and he’s got nothing to ride at the moment. So he can have it.
That’s kind. Does it need fixing first?
Only new brakes, and I can do that myself.
Good afternoon, Harbour Kitchen.
Hello. I booked a table for four on Friday at eight o’clock, under the name Patel. Unfortunately, two more friends would like to come, so there will be six of us now. Is that possible?
Let me check. Yes, we can move you to a bigger table, same day and same time.
Great, thank you very much.
I’ll make the sandwiches, and Kim is bringing the drinks. What about you?
I could do a salad.
Hmm, Kim’s mum is already making a big one, I think. Maybe something sweet?
Fruit, then. I’ll bring some melon and grapes.

items.question: What time will they meet?
items.why: He asks to meet at seven instead of half past six and she agrees. 7.40 would be six o'clock plus the bus journey.

items.question: What did Tom buy?
items.why: The blue jacket was not in his size, and he is waiting for the sale for the boots.

items.question: Where can the woman collect her umbrella?
items.why: The lost property office is closed until Monday, so the man keeps the umbrella at the ticket office.

items.question: What will the weather be like on Saturday?
options: Dry in the morning, then rainy
items.why: Saturday is dry in the morning with rain in the afternoon. Sunny is Friday and windy is Sunday.

items.question: What will the woman do with her old bike?
options: Take it to a repair shop
items.why: She decides against selling it, and she can fix the brakes herself.

items.question: Why is the man phoning the restaurant?
options: To ask for a different evening
To change the number of guests
items.why: He needs a table for six instead of four. Day and time stay the same.

items.question: What will the man bring to the picnic?
items.why: The woman makes the sandwiches, and the salad is already taken care of, so he brings fruit.

parts.title: Six short conversations
parts.instruction: You will hear six short conversations. For each question 8-13, choose the correct answer A, B or C. You will hear each conversation twice.

script.t: How’s the new gym? You joined last month, didn’t you?
Yes. To be honest, I’m not completely sure about it. It’s quite expensive, and the changing rooms are always crowded. But the instructors are fantastic.
So are you going to cancel?
No, no. I’ll give it a few more months and see.
Do you like working from home?
Mostly. There’s no journey to work, which is brilliant. But by Wednesday I start to feel a bit lonely, to be honest. I miss chatting to people at the coffee machine.
I can imagine.
Have you finished revising for tomorrow?
Yes, I’ve done all the past papers twice. I know the topics. It’s just that I know I’ll feel sick when I sit down in the exam room.
You’ll be fine. Try to get an early night.
What did you think of the film? I loved it.
The actors were great, I’ll say that. But it must have been nearly three hours long. I couldn’t wait for it to finish.
I’d like to return this jumper, please. It’s too small.
Do you have the receipt?
No, it was a present.
I’m afraid I can’t give you a refund then, and we haven’t got it in a larger size. But I can offer you a credit note for the same amount.
Hmm. Well, I did see a nice green scarf. Okay, a credit note is fine.
That building work starts at seven every morning. It’s driving me mad.
I know, but I don’t really mind. It will be finished by the autumn, and the new park will be so much nicer than that empty ground.
I suppose you’re right.

items.question: What does the woman think about her new gym?
options: She wants to cancel her membership.
She likes it, although some things annoy her.
She thinks the instructors are not good enough.
items.why: She mentions the price and crowded changing rooms, but the instructors are fantastic and she will stay a few more months.

items.question: What does the man say about working from home?
options: He would like to do it every day of the week.
He finds it hard to contact his boss.
items.why: By Wednesday he starts to feel lonely and misses chatting to colleagues.

items.question: How does the boy feel about tomorrow's exam?
options: He is well prepared but nervous.
He has not done enough work.
He is calm and does not care.
items.why: He has done all the past papers twice, but he is afraid he will feel sick in the exam room.

items.question: What did the man think of the film?
items.why: He praised the actors but said it was nearly three hours and he wanted it to finish.

items.question: What does the customer decide to do?
options: Exchange the jumper for a bigger size
items.why: No refund is possible without a receipt, and there is no larger size, so she takes the credit note.

items.question: Why doesn't the woman mind the building work?
options: She is out during the day.
She thinks the result will be good.
She can't hear much from her flat.
items.why: She says it will end by the autumn and the new park will be much nicer than the empty ground.

parts.title: Complete the notes
parts.instruction: You will hear a radio announcement about a community garden. For each question 14-19, write the missing information in the gap. You will hear the recording twice.

script.t: Good morning, and now some local news. The Riverside Community Garden is holding its open day, and everybody is invited. Some of you may have seen the first notice in the library, which gave the date as the seventh of June, but that was a mistake. The open day is on Saturday the fourteenth of June. The gates open at half past ten, not ten o’clock as it says on some leaflets, and they stay open until four.

Entry is free, and there is a café run by volunteers. Tea and coffee are a pound, and the homemade cakes are usually two pounds, but on open day they will be just one pound fifty each. Every visitor will also get a packet of seeds to take home. Last year it was tomato seeds, but this year it is sunflower seeds, so you will have something bright in your garden by August.
There is plenty for children, too. At eleven o’clock there will be plant pot painting, and at two o’clock children can make bird boxes with help from a local carpenter.

If you would like more information, or if you can help on the day, please phone the garden office on oh one six three two, nine six oh, four one eight. I’ll repeat that: oh one six three two, nine six oh, four one eight. Now, on with the music.

items.why: The first notice said the seventh, but that was a mistake. The correct date is the fourteenth.
The leaflets say ten o'clock, but the gates open at half past ten.

items.prompt: On open day, cakes cost £____ each.
items.why: Cakes are usually two pounds, but just one pound fifty on open day.

items.prompt: Every visitor gets a packet of ____ seeds.
items.why: Last year it was tomato seeds, but this year it is sunflower seeds.
Plant pot painting is at eleven. At two o'clock it is bird boxes.
The number is read out twice: oh one six three two, nine six oh, four one eight.

parts.title: A radio interview
parts.instruction: You will hear an interview with a man called Owen Hughes, who started a bicycle repair project. For each question 20-25, choose the correct answer A, B or C. You will hear the interview twice.

script.t: Welcome to Weekend Voices. My guest today is Owen Hughes, who started a bicycle repair project in Cardiff three years ago. Owen, welcome.
Thanks for having me.
How did it all begin?

Quite by accident. I’d worked in an office for ten years, and bikes were just a hobby. One weekend I fixed my neighbour’s bike in my garage, and word got round. Within a month I had a queue of people on my driveway.
So you thought, I’ll turn this into a business?

Not at all. People offered to pay, but I wouldn’t take any money. I was happy to help. It was the council who suggested a proper workshop. They offered me an empty room next to the market, and I couldn’t say no.
And do you charge now?
We ask for a donation, but it’s up to the customer. If somebody can’t afford to give anything, that’s fine. What matters is that they leave with a bike that works.
I hear you also teach people to repair bikes themselves.

Yes, and that’s the part I enjoy most. I love restoring old frames, of course, but every Thursday evening we have a class, and that’s the highlight of my week. Most people think they’ll be hopeless, but by the end of the first evening they can mend a puncture. I tell them it’s no harder than baking a cake.
Was there ever a time when you nearly gave up?

Last winter. We had a flood in the workshop and lost a lot of tools and spare parts. I was tired, and I thought, perhaps this is a sign. But the next morning twenty people turned up with buckets and brushes. I couldn’t walk away after that.
Some people say cycling in a city is dangerous.

I understand that. But I think the city is not so much dangerous as unprepared. If there were more safe lanes, more people would cycle, and drivers would get used to them. I’m not angry about it. I just think change takes time.
And what’s next for the project?

We’d like to open a second workshop on the other side of town, because our waiting list is long. But we need volunteers more than money. We have about fifteen at the moment, and we need at least double that.
Owen Hughes, thank you very much for talking to us.
My pleasure.

items.question: What made Owen open a proper workshop?
options: His neighbours paid him for repairs.
items.why: He refused payment, and he still worked in an office when it started. The council offered the room.

items.question: What does Owen say about payment at the workshop?
options: The council pays for the repairs.
items.why: The workshop asks for a donation, and someone who cannot pay anything is still helped.

items.question: What does Owen enjoy most about the work?
options: Teaching people to repair their own bikes
items.why: He loves restoring old frames, but he says the Thursday class is the part he enjoys most.

items.question: Why did Owen decide not to give up after the flood?
options: People came to help clear up.
items.why: Twenty people arrived with buckets and brushes the next morning.

items.question: What is Owen's opinion about cycling in cities?
options: It is too dangerous for most people.
Safer lanes would help, but change is slow.
items.why: He says the city is unprepared, more lanes would bring more cyclists, and that change takes time. He says he is not angry.

items.question: What does Owen need most for a second workshop?
items.why: He says they need volunteers more than money, and they need at least double the fifteen they have.

parts.title: Interview
parts.instruction: The examiner asks you some questions about yourself. Answer in a few sentences each. In the real test this part takes about two to three minutes.

tasks.title: Part 1 · Interview
tasks.situation: The examiner asks each candidate questions about their life, home, work or study, and free time.

card.title: Questions you might be asked
lines: Where do you live? What do you like about it?
What do you do? Do you like it?
What do you usually do at the weekend?
Tell me about a holiday you enjoyed.
What would you like to learn in the future?

redemittel: I live in … It’s a … place with …
I’m a … / I study …
What I like most about it is …
At the weekend I usually …, but sometimes I …
Last year I went to … with …
I’d really like to learn how to …
tasks.model: I live in a medium-sized town near the coast. What I like most about it is that it’s quiet but there’s still plenty to do. I work as a dental assistant, and I enjoy it because I meet different people every day. At the weekend I usually go for a long walk with my sister, and sometimes we cook dinner together. Last year I went to Portugal for a week, and the food was wonderful. In the future I’d really like to learn how to play the guitar.
checklist: Answer every question with more than one word, giving a reason or an example.
Use present simple for routines and past simple for the holiday.
Speak clearly, without long pauses.
Look at the examiner and be friendly.

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instruction: You are given a photograph and speak about it on your own for about one minute. Say where the people are, what they are doing and how they seem to feel. If you do not know a word, describe it in a different way. The examiner’s photograph is described on the card here.

tasks.title: Part 2 · Photograph: cooking together
tasks.situation: You have a photograph of two friends cooking together. Describe it for about a minute.

card.title: Photo: two friends in a kitchen
lines: What do they look like, and how do they seem to feel?
In the photo: two friends in a bright kitchen. One is stirring a pot, the other is cutting vegetables. Both are laughing. On the table there are plates and a bowl of fruit.

redemittel: In this photo I can see …
They are in …, perhaps at home.
On the left / on the right / in the background …
One of them is … -ing, and the other one is … -ing.
They look happy / relaxed because …
I think they might be …
tasks.model: In this photo I can see two friends in a bright kitchen. It looks like a home kitchen, perhaps one of their flats. On the left a young man is stirring something in a big pot, and on the right a woman is cutting vegetables. They are both laughing, so I think they are having a good time. There are plates and a bowl of fruit on the table, so perhaps they are going to eat together soon. I think they might be good friends, because they seem very relaxed with each other. I enjoy cooking with friends too, because it makes the evening more fun.
checklist: Say where the people are, what they are doing, and how they look or feel.
Use present continuous (are cooking, is stirring) and position words (on the left, in the background).
Use 'perhaps', 'I think' and 'might' when you are not sure.
Keep talking for about a minute; if a word is missing, describe it in other words.

parts.title: Talk together: choose a present
parts.instruction: You and your partner talk together for two to three minutes. A colleague is leaving the company. Talk about the presents on the card and decide together which one is best. You do not need to agree at once, but try to reach a decision.

tasks.title: Part 3 · A leaving present
tasks.situation: A colleague is leaving the company after five years. You and your partner want to buy a leaving present from the whole team.

card.title: Which present is best?
lines: A plant for the new home
A photo album of the team

redemittel: What do you think about …?
I think … would be a good idea because …
That’s true, but …
I’m not sure about that. How about …?
Why don’t we …?
So, shall we choose …? / Let’s go for …, then.
tasks.model: A: Shall we start with the book about travelling? B: Maybe, but I don’t know if she likes reading. How about a photo album of the team? A: That’s a lovely idea because she can remember us, but it takes a lot of time to make. B: That’s true. What do you think about a voucher for a café? A: I’m not sure. It’s a bit impersonal. Why don’t we give her tickets for a concert? She loves music. B: Good point, but we don’t know what she likes. A: Then let’s go for the photo album, and we can all write a message in it. B: Great, let’s do that.
checklist: Talk about most of the pictures and give a reason for your opinion.
Ask your partner questions and react to what they say.
Make suggestions and agree or disagree politely.
Reach a decision at the end.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.instruction: The examiner asks you and your partner some more questions on the topic of Part 3 (presents and celebrations). Give your own opinion and listen to your partner. This part takes about three minutes.

tasks.title: Part 4 · Presents and celebrations
tasks.situation: The examiner continues the topic of presents and celebrations.

card.title: Questions you might be asked
lines: Do you like giving presents? Why or why not?
What was the best present you have ever received?
Do you think people spend too much money on presents?
How do you like to celebrate your birthday?

redemittel: Personally, I think …
In my opinion, …
I agree / I don’t really agree, because …
For example, …
What about you?
I’ve never thought about that, but I suppose …
tasks.model: Personally, I love giving presents, because I enjoy seeing people’s faces when they open them. The best present I have ever received was a small notebook from my grandmother. She wrote a message on the first page, and I still use it. I think some people do spend too much money on presents, for example at Christmas, when shops are full of things nobody needs. For my birthday I like a quiet evening with a few close friends and a nice meal. What about you?
checklist: Give your opinion and a reason or example for each answer.
Listen to your partner and respond to what they said.
Ask your partner a question as well.
Aim for clear pronunciation and a range of vocabulary.
